newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Liberty to boost its Regent Street store.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Liberty to boost its Regent Street store.

text.p: British retailer Liberty Plc, known for its fine fabrics, on Friday announced plans to redevelop its upmarket Regent Street store in London's West End at a cost of around 40 million pounds ($65.3 million).
"Certainly the engine for growth is to build on the success of Regent Street," chairman Denis Cassidy told Reuters.
The purpose of the redevelopment, which will boost trading space by around 50 percent, is twofold, group managing director Ian Thomson told Reuters.

Firstly, it will allow the expansion of the current range of merchandise like cosmetics, footwear, household textiles and fashion. And secondly, it will enable new categories such as food, beauty services and lingerie to be introduced.
The Regent Street store's trading performance has picked up with sales rising by two percent in the first half of last year and eight percent in the second half, and is higher still now.
"It strengthened fairly substantially towards the end of the year and that trend has been continued into the current trading year, hovering just below a double digit increase," Thomson said.
The cost of the redevelopment will be met by an increase in borrowing facilities and from the group's strong cash position.
"The investment in Regent Street should have a substantial impact on profitability," Cassidy said in a telephone interview.

Liberty is also looking to expand its airport shops. It has four shops currently at London's Heathrow airport, which it sees playing a key role in promoting the Liberty brand and acting as a bridge to consumers outside Britain.
"Gatwick North in the medium term could be an interesting possibility," said Thomson, when asked if Liberty could expand its airport shops.
Numerous contacts have also been made with airports around the world and Thomson expects "some progress in the coming year".

The company also reported a return to the black after a huge restructuring programme, which is now almost complete. Pretax profit was 4.4 million pounds in the year to February 1, compared with last year's loss of 16.6 million pounds when an exceptional charge of 18.7 million pounds was made for the restructuring.

Following a strategic view last year Liberty decided to stop making and distributing its distinctive fabrics, selling licences to others to do so instead. It opted, however, to keep designing its paisley prints and other fabrics.
The restructuring that followed saw Liberty close its 20 branch shops in Britain, withdraw from its European textile operations and shut its warehouse in Burnley, northern England.

"The certainty with which we've implemented the programme and the success with which it's been achieved are quite reassuring pointers to what I hope we'll achieve in the next year as we begin to build much more for the future instead of concentrating on clearing up the past," said Cassidy.
While the Regent Street store is the company's focus in the near term, building the Liberty brand and its expansion in both domestic and international markets is the longer-term goal.
"The development of the Liberty brand holds the key to the future," Cassidy said in the results statement.
Liberty restored its dividend with a final payment of 1.85 pence per share, which equates to a maintained dividend for the year as a whole.

The board seeks a dividend policy more closely related to earnings than in the past, while taking a conservative degree of cover owing to cash needs for its redevelopment plans. It intends to pay an interim dividend of about 30 percent of any intended total. Cassidy said 1996/97's 1.85 pence is "broadly equivalent to about 2.7/2.9 pence for a full year had we paid an interim".
Liberty's share price on the London Stock Exchange showed no change at 370 pence by 1140 GMT.
($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
